title: Photonic realization of a subgraph extraction in a quantum random network
authors: Lijun Xia, Xuemei Gu, Kai Wang, Leizhen Chen, Mario Krenn, Yan-Qing Lu, Shining Zhu, Xiao-Song Ma
abstract: Understanding how complex connectivity emerges in networks is a fundamental challenge in classical and quantum science. In classical random networks, complex subgraphs typically require relatively high connection probabilities, whereas quantum random network theory predicts that such structures can arise at a single, lower threshold through entanglement and local operations. Here, using an integrated silicon photonic chip, we experimentally realize a quantum subgraph predicted by quantum random network theory in a four-node quantum random network. Our integrated platform exploits probabilistic photon-pair sources and coherent control of path modes to prepare a structured quantum subgraph through local transformations and postselection, operating in a threshold regime that differs from classical random networks. We verify that the subgraph state exhibits genuine high-dimensional multipartite entanglement across the nodes, providing experimental evidence that quantum entanglement enables connectivity structures beyond classical accessibility.
summary: The research experimentally realizes a specific quantum subgraph within a quantum random network using an integrated silicon photonic chip. By exploiting entangled photon pairs and local operations, the authors demonstrate connectivity patterns achievable only through quantum entanglement, validating predictions from QRN theory over classical models.
main_problem: The study aims to experimentally realize a quantum subgraph structure predicted by quantum random network theory, contrasting this with classical connectivity thresholds.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the preparation of a specific finite quantum subgraph ($\lambda$ graph) using an integrated photonic chip, confirming that entanglement enables connectivity structures inaccessible classically.
method: The experiment uses probabilistic photon-pair sources and local transformations on an integrated silicon photonic chip, followed by mode-selective postselection to extract the desired entangled state.
model_or_system: The physical platform is an integrated silicon photonic chip utilizing spontaneous four-wave mixing for generating Bell-state links. The theoretical framework compares classical random graphs (Erdős–Rényi) with Quantum Random Networks (QRN).
key_observables: Fidelity ($F_{\exp}$), entanglement witness values ($W$), and visibility measurements (RHOM/HHOM contrast/visibility).
important_parameters: The experiment operates in a regime distinct from the large-$N$ threshold scaling, focusing on finite subgraph realization.
main_assumptions: The protocol relies on probabilistic photon-pair sources and postselection; the fidelity calculations assume measurement capability across all required projections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup using integrated photonic circuits, schematic protocols for state preparation (e.g., four-node module), and interference patterns used for characterization.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical difference between classical and quantum network connectivity to detailing the physical implementation on a silicon chip, followed by rigorous measurements of entanglement dimensionality using fidelity and visibility witnesses.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete experimental evidence in photonics that harnesses genuine multipartite entanglement to engineer complex quantum structures predicted by advanced network theories, bridging fundamental theory with scalable hardware.

Figure 2. Overview of the experiment and the integrated photonic circuit. Two picosecond pump pulses at different wavelengths are coupled into the chip via a grating coupler and equally distributed to eight DMZI-Rs. Within the DMZI-Rs, the pump pulses (1544.78 nm and 1556.84 nm) generate photon pairs at 1550.81 nm through spontaneous four-wave mixing. The photons are then routed through delay lines that match their arrival times and establish coherent node-to-node connections, preparing the resource state |G⟩(after the white dashed line).
